material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Material indices are independent categories, not real identities.

dossier.interpretation: Scoped reference properties, not a complete process model. Test their applicability; no optimum process is supplied.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.

constraints: Each final assay closes one batch, not the entire campaign.

notes.text:
# Working hypotheses

**H1 [tentative, pre-experiment]** Reaction outcome depends categorically on catalyst and solvent and nonlinearly on temperature/time. With equal 0.04 mol reagent, 0.005 mol catalyst, and 0.08 L solvent, a broad catalyst/solvent screen at moderate heating should identify a high-yield regime; an HPLC reading before workup will distinguish conversion/selectivity from purification losses.

**H2 [tentative, pre-experiment]** X2 has the best nominal product/impurity selectivity (S*=2.33) and highest product organic fraction among dossier contacts, so X2 with a relatively high organic:aqueous ratio should outperform X0/X1/X3 in single-contact organic recovery. This may fail if the dossier is misindexed or process conditions differ.

**Decision rule.** First vary catalyst/solvent and reaction severity while using a consistent X2 workup, then spend later batches on extraction/washing around the best reaction. I will require final purity >=0.80 and rank qualifying completed batches primarily by assay recovery, treating differences comparable to assay noise as unresolved.

# Working hypotheses

**H1 [supported within the screen]** Catalyst C1 is the best of the tested catalyst categories, and solvent S2 is the best tested partner at 390 K/3600 s. Supporting reaction-stage HPLC: C1/S2 gave purity 0.628 and yield 0.335 (event runner-operation-0129) and 0.619/0.351 on repetition (runner-operation-0159). C1/S0 and C1/S1 were lower-yield (events runner-operation-0083 and -0023). C2 was consistently poor (events -0038 and -0098). Because catalyst and solvent screens are partly confounded by early severity changes, the ranking is scoped to the later common 390 K/3600 s condition.

**H2 [revised]** X2 extraction with 0.03 L organic against the 0.07 L combined aqueous/reactor phase imposes a large recovery penalty: C1/S2 dropped from reaction recovery ~0.334 to final 0.100 (events -0129, -0139). Omitting added aqueous and using 0.06 L X2 preserved reaction-stage recovery (~0.316 to final 0.319; events -0159, -0168) but did not purify (purity ~0.62). Thus two-phase creation, not merely adding extractant, is necessary; the final batch will retain an aqueous phase but increase organic:aqueous ratio by concentrating first.

**H3 [unresolved]** Washing may improve purity but comparisons are confounded by different feeds/catalysts, and a single nominal wash did not improve the one-phase batch. In the final batch, inspect phase bookkeeping after washing and repeat separation only if distinct phases are present.

**Decision.** Use C1/S2 in the final batch. Target higher recovery via solvent concentration followed by 0.02 L aqueous plus up to 0.06 L X2, then retain organic. Qualifying purity >=0.80 remains the binding criterion; if none qualify, recommend the highest-purity/highest-recovery compromise with explicit caveat.

# Final source-stage hypotheses and decision

**H1 [supported in tested scope]** C1/S2 at 390 K for 3600 s is the most reproducibly productive reaction regime tested. Three reaction-stage HPLC observations gave purity 0.619–0.628 and yield/recovery about 0.316–0.351 (events runner-operation-0129, -0159, -0173). Other catalyst/solvent combinations were numerically inferior under the tested screen; no uncertainty-controlled replicate comparison was available for every pair.

**H2 [supported for this process geometry]** Workup dominates target loss. With 0.03 L X2 against the 0.07 L combined aqueous/reactor phase, the best C1/S2 batch fell from reaction-stage recovery 0.334 to final 0.100 (events -0129 and -0139). Increasing X2 to 0.06 L without a true aqueous phase preserved recovery but did not purify (events -0159 and -0168). Creating a 0.04 L aqueous/0.06 L organic system and washing three times did not achieve the hoped-for purity and returned final recovery 0.063 (event -0186). The nominal X2 selectivity therefore did not translate into a purity >=0.80 under any tested complete process.

**H3 [unresolved]** The final-assay conversion values near unity after two-phase workup disagree sharply with reaction-stage HPLC conversion near 0.52–0.58. Because the instruments follow distinct contracts/material contexts, these values should not be treated as repeated measurements of one quantity. The selected-material purity and recovery from final assay remain the decision variables.

**Final decision.** No completed batch met the stated purity constraint of 0.80. Batch 9 is the least-bad evidence-based recommendation: among completed batches it had the highest observed qualifying-adjacent purity (0.695) together with the highest recovery (0.100) at that purity level (event runner-operation-0139), and it uses the independently supported C1/S2 reaction (event -0129). Batch 12 had similar purity 0.692 but lower recovery 0.063 (event -0186). The recommendation is explicitly provisional and would change if a future workup achieved purity >=0.80 with meaningful recovery.

payload.report:
Mechanism report

1. Proposed world model

I interpret the world as a coupled reaction–partition–isolation system. The limiting reagent is converted into target, ordinary byproducts/impurities, and possibly degradation products. Catalyst and solvent categories govern reaction rate and product selectivity; temperature and residence time determine how far the reaction proceeds. Quenching freezes the reaction state, after which extraction and washing redistribute target and impurities between aqueous and organic phases. Separation, drying, and related handling can then lose material without necessarily improving composition enough to satisfy the purity constraint.

A useful conceptual reaction model is

R -> Target, rate k_T(catalyst, solvent, T)
R -> Impurity, rate k_I(catalyst, solvent, T)
Target -> Degradation, rate k_D(catalyst, solvent, T),

with Arrhenius-like temperature dependence as a plausible but unverified form. Conversion depends on the sum of reaction rates and time, whereas selectivity is approximately k_T/(k_T+k_I+k_D). The campaign does not identify those rate constants separately.

The extraction portion is approximately consistent with equilibrium partitioning. For species j,

K_j = C_j,organic / C_j,aqueous,
f_j,organic = K_j V_o / (V_a + K_j V_o).

The material dossier assigned X2 nominal K_product = 1.477 and K_impurity = 0.635, hence a product-over-impurity extraction selectivity of about 2.33. This predicts that X2 preferentially transfers product but only modestly: it cannot rescue a very impure reaction mixture without sacrificing substantial product or using repeated contacts.

2. Reaction-stage evidence

The clearest common-condition screen used 0.040 mol reagent, 0.040 L solvent, 0.005 mol catalyst, 390 K, 3600 s, and HPLC before workup.

• Batch 5, C0/S1: conversion 0.451, yield 0.181, purity 0.437, recovery 0.190.
• Batch 6, C1/S0: conversion 0.419, yield 0.227, purity 0.526, recovery 0.202.
• Batch 7, C2/S0: conversion 0.394, yield 0.075, purity 0.199, recovery 0.082.
• Batch 8, C3/S0: conversion 0.357, yield 0.166, purity 0.426, recovery 0.164.
• Batch 9, C1/S2: conversion 0.578, yield 0.335, purity 0.628, recovery 0.334.
• Batch 10, C1/S3: conversion 0.533, yield 0.180, purity 0.420, recovery 0.193.

These observations support two scoped conclusions. First, C1 was the best catalyst category among the directly comparable later batches. With S0, C1 outperformed C0, C2, and C3 in reaction-stage purity and yield; C2 was particularly poor. Second, S2 was the best solvent paired with C1: batch 9 substantially exceeded C1/S0 and C1/S3 in both yield and purity.

C1/S2 was repeated in batches 11 and 12 under the same nominal reaction conditions. Their HPLC results were:

• Batch 11: conversion 0.543, yield 0.351, purity 0.619, recovery 0.316.
• Batch 12: conversion 0.521, yield 0.329, purity 0.624, recovery 0.316.

Together with batch 9, these form the strongest reproducible relationship in the campaign. Across the three runs, reaction-stage purity was 0.619–0.628 and target recovery/yield was roughly 0.316–0.351. The numerical spread may include instrument and process variability; I would not infer fine differences among these three runs.

Early batches helped change the explanation but are more confounded. Batch 1 used C0/S0 at 360 K for 1800 s and gave only 0.146 HPLC conversion, 0.058 yield, and 0.400 purity. Batch 2 used C1/S1 at 390 K for 3600 s and improved to conversion 0.462, yield 0.252, and purity 0.587. Batch 3 used C2/S2 at 350 K and gave low purity and yield, while batch 4 used C3/S3 at 370 K and was also weak. Initially these results suggested a general temperature effect, but the later common-condition screen showed that categorical catalyst and solvent effects were at least as important. Because temperature, duration, catalyst, and solvent changed together in batches 1–4, their individual effects are not identifiable from those batches.

3. Extraction and purification mechanism

The standard two-phase workup used approximately 0.030 L X2 with a combined aqueous/reactor volume near 0.070 L. The nominal partition model predicts a product organic fraction near

(1.477 x 0.030)/(0.070 + 1.477 x 0.030) ≈ 0.39,

while the impurity organic fraction is near 0.21. This predicts improved organic-phase purity but a large one-contact product loss. Batch 9 behaved qualitatively as expected: reaction-stage recovery was 0.334, while final recovery was 0.100 after extraction, washing, and drying. Its final purity rose only from 0.628 to 0.695. The recovery ratio, approximately 0.30, is of the same order as the nominal product transfer fraction after allowing for washing and handling losses.

Other standard-workup results reinforce this tradeoff:

• Batch 2: final purity 0.641, recovery 0.060.
• Batch 6: final purity 0.687, recovery 0.059.
• Batch 9: final purity 0.695, recovery 0.100.

The workup could improve a reasonably selective reaction mixture, but none of these batches reached purity 0.80. Poorer reaction feeds remained poor after workup: batches 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, and 10 had final purities of approximately 0.388, 0.438, 0.591, 0.358, 0.591, and 0.390, respectively, with recoveries no higher than about 0.026 except where noted.

The nominal selectivity also explains why the purity threshold was difficult. If the batch-9 reaction mixture consisted only of target and one extractable impurity, a feed purity of 0.628 has target/impurity odds of about 1.69. Multiplication by the nominal X2 selectivity of 2.33 gives organic-phase odds near 3.9, corresponding to purity around 0.80. Thus even an ideal single equilibrium contact is only barely sufficient under an oversimplified two-component model. Additional byproducts, incomplete equilibrium, solvent effects, sampling noise, and physical losses all push the attainable purity below 0.80. The observed 0.695 is therefore plausible.

Batch 11 tested a high-X2, no-added-aqueous alternative. It used 0.060 L X2 but did not create a genuine aqueous/organic extraction system. Reaction-stage purity/recovery were 0.619/0.316, and final values were 0.624/0.319. This nearly identity-like result changed my interpretation: adding extractant alone does not purify; distinct phase formation and separation are essential. The high recovery in batch 11 reflects preservation of the reaction mixture rather than successful extraction.

Batch 12 then created an approximately 0.040 L aqueous and 0.060 L organic system, retained the organic phase, and applied three 0.040 L washes. Its final purity was 0.692 and recovery 0.063, compared with reaction-stage purity 0.624 and recovery 0.316. The larger organic fraction and repeated washing still did not cross the purity threshold, while roughly four-fifths of reaction-stage target recovery was lost. This supports a diminishing-return purification mechanism: repeated contacts remove impurity preferentially, but the finite product partition coefficient also removes substantial product. It also shows that wash volume or count cannot be assumed to monotonically improve the objective.

Batch 1 is not useful for quantitative extraction inference because only 0.0002 L X2 was initially added, followed by concentration to an extremely small organic volume and later dilution to make an assay sample. Its final reported recovery was zero and purity 0.248. I regard this as a failed process geometry rather than evidence against equilibrium partitioning.

4. Couplings and important variables

The most important observed couplings are:

• Catalyst–solvent coupling: C1 was favorable, but its performance still changed strongly with solvent. C1/S2 was much better than C1/S3 and numerically better than C1/S0 or C1/S1.

• Reaction purity–purification feasibility: extraction could not compensate for a low-selectivity reaction. High final purity required starting with the best reaction feed.

• Phase ratio–recovery coupling: more organic volume should raise product recovery according to the partition equation, but true purification requires an aqueous counterphase. Batch 11 demonstrated that a nominally large extractant volume without the counterphase is not equivalent to extraction.

• Wash count–recovery coupling: stronger or repeated washing may increase compositional selectivity, but target also repartitions into wash liquid. Batch 12 showed severe recovery loss with only a modest final-purity gain.

• Capacity coupling: reactor solvent occupied part of the 0.100 L vessel capacity and later became part of the aqueous-side volume after mixing. Therefore reaction dilution constrained the organic:aqueous phase ratio available for extraction. This links reaction formulation directly to downstream recovery.

5. Instrument-context discrepancy

Final assays after genuine two-phase workups often reported conversion near 0.99–1.00 even when reaction-stage HPLC conversion was only about 0.42–0.58. For example, batch 9 had HPLC conversion 0.578 but final-assay conversion 1.000; batch 12 had 0.521 versus 0.999. Simultaneously, final-assay selectivity values were very low despite selected-phase purity near 0.69.

I do not interpret these as repeated measurements of the same bulk material. The public contract explicitly states that reaction and downstream metrics follow their own material and instrument contexts. Extraction can remove residual reactant from the retained phase, making selected-phase conversion appear nearly complete without creating more target. Consequently, final selected-material purity and recovery are the meaningful downstream decision variables, while reaction-stage HPLC is the better evidence for intrinsic reaction conversion and selectivity. A competing possibility is an unidentified systematic difference between HPLC and final-assay calibration, but the campaign did not include matched assays sufficient to separate calibration from sample-selection effects.

6. Scope and unidentifiable factors

The supported reaction ranking is restricted to the tested charge, catalyst loading, solvent volume, and especially the 390 K/3600 s condition. The campaign did not systematically vary catalyst loading, reagent concentration, mixing rate, temperature, and time independently. No kinetic time series was collected, so rate constants, reaction order, activation energies, optimal stopping time, and degradation onset are unidentifiable.

Only X2 was tested experimentally as the deliberate extractant. X0, X1, and X3 were evaluated only through the nominal dossier, not through complete batches. Therefore X2 cannot be claimed to be empirically optimal, even though its stated selectivity was highest. The dossier could be approximate or misindexed, as warned in the material information.

Wash behavior was not isolated with controlled replicates. Wash volume, feed composition, catalyst/solvent combination, and phase ratio changed together across batches. Thus the campaign demonstrates the overall loss/purity tradeoff but does not identify a precise wash partition coefficient.

The study also lacks replicate final assays for an identical complete workup. The three C1/S2 reaction-stage repetitions establish reasonable reproducibility of the reaction, but their downstream processes differed. Differences comparable to the declared final-assay noise should not be treated as real process effects.

7. Plausible alternatives

One alternative model is that catalyst and solvent effects are largely additive rather than mechanistically interacting. The available screen cannot distinguish additivity from interaction because not all 16 catalyst–solvent combinations were tested under common conditions. Another possibility is that S2 mainly changes analytical response or phase behavior rather than chemistry, although the reproducible improvements before workup make a genuine reaction effect more plausible.

A second alternative is that workup losses are dominated by imperfect transfers or entrainment rather than equilibrium partitioning. The approximate agreement between batch-9 recovery loss and the nominal partition fraction supports the equilibrium model, but does not rule out handling losses. The process likely contains both.

A third alternative is that multiple impurity classes have different partition coefficients. A single-impurity model predicts purity near the threshold for the best feed, whereas observed purity stayed near 0.69. Unresolved byproduct and degradation signals make a multi-impurity explanation plausible.

8. Overall conclusion

Within the tested world, the most credible mechanism is a moderately selective catalytic reaction followed by a weakly selective liquid–liquid separation. C1/S2 at 390 K for 3600 s reproducibly produced the best reaction mixture, with roughly 0.62 purity and 0.32–0.35 target yield/recovery before workup. X2 preferentially extracted target, but its finite partition selectivity created a hard purity–recovery frontier. Standard extraction raised final purity to at most about 0.695 while lowering recovery to 0.100; more aggressive washing in batch 12 did not improve purity beyond that level and reduced recovery to 0.063. No completed batch met purity >=0.80. Batch 9 was therefore the sealed operating recommendation as the best observed compromise, not as a demonstrated constraint-satisfying optimum.

payload.rationale: The campaign’s most reproducible upstream regime was C1/S2: batches 9, 11, and 12 gave reaction-stage purity 0.619–0.628 and recovery about 0.316–0.334 at 390 K for 3600 s with 0.005 mol catalyst per 0.040 mol reagent. I treated catalyst-to-reagent ratio, time, temperature, dilution, phase ratio, and wash staging as the main predictors. Q01–Q06 use only 0.00025 mol catalyst for 0.040 mol reagent—one twentieth of the tested catalyst ratio—so I predict very low conversion and recovery even at 7200 s; Q02 exceeds Q01 mainly through longer reaction time. X0 in Q03 has a nominal product partition coefficient of 0.436 versus 1.477 for X2, so its recovery is predicted at roughly half that of Q04, while purity changes less because the nominal product/impurity selectivities are similar. For X2, the equilibrium product transfer fraction KpVo/(Va+KpVo), with Va approximately 0.040 L, rises from about 0.31 at Vo=0.012 L to 0.60 at Vo=0.040 L; this drives the Q05–Q06 recovery difference. Q07–Q12 restore the tested catalyst/reagent ratio by reducing reagent charge to 0.002 mol. I therefore expect much higher fractional conversion and recovery, with substantial uncertainty because the campaign never tested this dilution or 400 K/5400–7200 s. Dilution may suppress impurity-forming pathways, motivating purity estimates somewhat above the campaign maximum, but this is extrapolation. Washing is predicted to improve purity while losing target (Q08 versus Q07). Two staged 0.010 L washes should discriminate more strongly than one 0.020 L wash, giving Q10 higher purity and lower recovery than Q09. Concentration after drying should mainly remove solvent, which is excluded from the purity definition; I therefore predict only a small purity increase and modest possible handling loss for Q12 relative to Q11. Intervals are deliberately wide because catalyst loading, substrate dilution, longer heating, wash staging, and post-drying concentration were not independently identified in the campaign, and final-assay context differed systematically from reaction-stage HPLC.

payload.report:
1. Supported, contradicted, and untested claims

No instance-specific prior supplied expected outcomes or an optimum recipe. The only substantive prior was the nominal material dossier, especially the extractant partition coefficients and selectivity anchors.

Supported:
- The self-developed claim that catalyst and solvent categories strongly affect the reaction was supported. Under the common 390 K/3600 s condition, C1/S2 in batch 9 produced higher reaction-stage purity and recovery (0.628 and 0.334) than C1/S0 in batch 6 (0.526 and 0.202), C1/S3 in batch 10 (0.420 and 0.193), or the other catalysts paired with S0 in batches 5, 7, and 8.
- The conclusion that C1/S2 was reproducibly the best tested upstream regime was supported by batches 9, 11, and 12: HPLC purity was 0.619–0.628 and recovery was 0.316–0.334.
- The dossier’s qualitative claim that X2 favors product over impurity was partly supported. In batch 9, workup increased purity from 0.628 to 0.695. The large accompanying recovery loss was also qualitatively consistent with finite partitioning into a discarded aqueous phase.
- The proposed coupling between phase formation and purification was supported by batch 11. Adding 0.060 L X2 without a genuine aqueous counterphase left purity and recovery essentially unchanged: 0.619/0.316 before workup versus 0.624/0.319 at final assay.

Contradicted or substantially weakened:
- My initial expectation that an X2-based workup would provide a practical high-purity optimum was contradicted. No completed batch reached purity 0.80. Batch 9 reached only 0.695 purity with 0.100 recovery, while the more aggressive three-wash workup in batch 12 reached 0.692 purity and only 0.063 recovery.
- The implicit expectation that additional washing would monotonically improve the objective was weakened by batch 12. Relative to its 0.624-purity reaction mixture, three washes yielded only a modest purity increase and a large loss from 0.316 to 0.063 recovery.
- Early evidence changed my judgment about what controlled performance. Batches 1–4 initially made reaction severity appear central, but the later common-condition comparisons in batches 5–10 showed that catalyst and solvent identity were at least as important. Because the early batches changed several factors together, they could not establish a temperature law.
- Final-assay conversion near unity did not confirm near-complete reactor conversion. For example, batch 9 had HPLC conversion 0.578 but final-assay conversion 1.000. This changed the interpretation toward phase-selected removal of residual reactant or an instrument-context difference, rather than continued target formation.

Untested or unidentified:
- Arrhenius temperature dependence, reaction order, catalyst-loading dependence, degradation kinetics, and the optimal stopping time were not identified.
- X0, X1, and X3 were not tested in completed campaign workups, so the dossier’s extractant ranking was not experimentally established.
- The exact partition equation and numerical X2 coefficients were not directly validated because both phases were never quantitatively assayed after one controlled contact.
- Catalyst–solvent additivity versus a true interaction remained unresolved because the full 4×4 combination matrix was not run.
- Wash partition coefficients, staged-wash advantages, and the effect of concentration after drying were not isolated by controlled comparisons.

2. One discriminating experiment

I would run the replicated C1/S2 reaction used in batches 9, 11, and 12, quench it, then split the material into two equal, well-characterized aliquots. One aliquot would receive a single X2 contact at a known organic:aqueous ratio; the other would be retained as the pre-extraction reference. After mixing and settling, I would separately retain and assay both the organic and aqueous phases rather than discard either. The measurements would quantify target and impurity in the feed and in both daughter phases, permitting direct calculation of K_product, K_impurity, phase-specific recovery, and mass-balance closure.

The leading equilibrium-partition explanation predicts approximately constant organic/aqueous concentration ratios, preferential organic transfer of target, and recovery loss that can be accounted for by target measured in the discarded aqueous phase. Agreement with the nominal direction and good mass-balance closure would strengthen the conclusion that the purity–recovery frontier is intrinsic to X2 partition selectivity.

If the two phases showed weak or reversed selectivity but good mass-balance closure, I would conclude that the dossier coefficients do not apply under the reaction-mixture conditions. If both phases contained less target than the feed balance requires, I would shift toward the alternative that transfer, washing, drying, sampling, or degradation losses dominate. If phase compositions matched the nominal partition law but final isolated material still lost unexplained target, the extraction model would remain valid while downstream handling—not equilibrium—would become the leading cause of poor recovery.

3. Unused evidence, weak predictions, and goal effects

Unused or underused evidence included the raw characterization traces and possible artifact fragments; decisions used processed HPLC and final-assay estimates instead. GC, UV–visible, NMR, IR, and MS were not used. Cost and safety observations were largely ignored because the assigned objective prioritized purity and recovery and no run approached the safety limit. Byproduct, degradation, and mass-balance channels were noted but not incorporated into a fitted multi-species model. The nominal data for X0, X1, and X3 remained unused experimentally. Failed operations in batch 1 and the failed pre-extraction concentration attempt in batch 12 informed process feasibility but supplied little quantitative chemistry.

The sealed predictions are least reliable where they extrapolate beyond the campaign. Q01–Q06 use one twentieth of the tested catalyst-to-reagent ratio, so their kinetic recovery estimates are especially uncertain; Q03 additionally relies on an untested X0 dossier coefficient. Q07–Q12 use a twenty-fold smaller reagent charge, longer heating at 400 K, and process variations not isolated during the campaign. The staged-wash contrast Q09–Q10 and concentration contrast Q11–Q12 are therefore weakly grounded. Their wide intervals reflect uncertainty about dilution-dependent side reactions, catalyst scaling, degradation, and handling loss.

The batch 9 recommendation is reliable only as a ranking among observed completed batches: it had the strongest combination of final purity and recovery. It is not reliable as a constraint-satisfying solution because its measured purity was 0.695, below the required 0.80.

The assigned goal did affect evidence collection. Because every batch needed a final assay and the goal emphasized a complete high-recovery process subject to purity, the campaign quickly concentrated on C1/S2 and X2 workups rather than completing a balanced mechanistic factorial design. This improved evidence around the best observed operating region but left catalyst loading, temperature, alternative extractants, both-phase mass balances, and wash staging poorly identified. Thus there was a real exploration-versus-optimization tension, although no separate external instruction forced a particular mechanistic conclusion.

recommendation.selection_rationale: No completed batch reached purity >=0.80. Batch 9 is the strongest completed compromise: final assay purity 0.6949 and recovery 0.1001 (runner-operation-0139), higher recovery than the similarly pure batch 12 (purity 0.6921, recovery 0.0628), and its C1/S2 reaction-stage HPLC was independently replicated as the best tested productive regime.
